newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Venezuela faces OPEC dilemma of conflicting needs.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela faces OPEC dilemma of conflicting needs.

text.p: Venezuela, OPEC's semi-detached member, will once again offer a new production strategy for the oil producers' group at its ministerial meeting which begins here on Wednesday.

Driven by economic need at home and convinced that OPEC's production quota system has outlived its usefulness, Venezuela has suggested, more publicly in recent months, that OPEC follow a more contemporary, market-driven approach.
OPEC delegates say other OPEC members will listen to Venezuela's proposal this week on separating domestic demand from quotas but is not likely to approve it.
"Demand is demand no matter from where it comes. It is all part of the global supply-demand picture," said an OPEC delegate.
Before OPEC's last meeting in June this year oil minister Erwin Arrieta floated his "New World Energy Map" idea, whereby OPEC members would concentrate more on nearby markets.
That was not taken seriously by fellow members like Saudi Arabia who believe that OPEC can not carve up the world market and dictate from where consumers should buy their oil.
Venezuela's problem is how to marry its obligations as a cartel member with its ambitious campaign to woo foreign investment in its ever-expanding oil industry.
Such a dilemma is one faced by several of OPEC's cash-strapped members, confronted by social unrest and increasing competion from rival oil producers.
Luis Giusti, head of state oil company Petroleos de Venezuela (PdVSA), made clear last week the emphasis Venezuela places on the commercial realities.
"We will continue to increase our production according to market conditions and our international obligations," he told an audience of international oil executives in Caracas.
Venezuela's obligation to OPEC is to feed the market no more than 2.359 million barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil.
But this has long been ignored.

Official figures obtained by Reuters recently showed the founding OPEC member expects to export 2.739 million bpd of crude and refined oil products this year, rising to 3.03 million bpd next year. And that doesn't include domestic consumption, which is running at about 400,000 bpd.

Giusti, widely seen as the brains behind his country's oil strategy, sees production rising to 5.7 million bpd over the next 10 years, with Venezuela capturing more than twice the rate of world demand growth over the period.

Venezuela therefore aims to recapture some of the market share lost to non-OPEC producers in recent years when the group has tried to stick to a production ceiling. Giusti is on record as saying that OPEC's "confused" policy can't hope to control production or prices.
"Venezuela is trying to recast OPEC in what might be said to be a modern mould," said Robert Bottome, an analyst at VenEconomy, a Caracas-based consultancy.

"The question you have to ask is what is OPEC's role in the world. If it is a quota-setting cartel then it is fair to say that Venezuela has nothing to do with it," he added. "If it is a strategic-planning entity, a community of interests trying to look for common policies then it has a tremendously important role."
Venezuela's overriding imperative is an economic crisis which culminated in an IMF-backed economic adjustment plan in April of this year.

Windfall oil revenues this year of around $3 billion, thanks to higher prices and quota-busting production, are to go exclusively to paying foreign debt, Venezuela's planning minister said earlier this month.
"It is really (Giusti's) idea that expansion of the oil sector makes substantial commercial sense," said Raphael Qijano, a director of Petroleum Finance Co in Washington D.C.
"Venezuela is looking at a production pattern that is growing independent of OPEC because it has these huge reserves and sees prices in real terms staying flat long-term," Qijano added.
Venezuela early this year allowed foreign oil companies for the first time in 20 years to bid for major exploration licences, with the expectation that they will add 500,000 bpd to production.

PdVSA also continues to build its downstream portfolio, which had refining capacity at the end of 1995 of more than 3.3 million bpd, spread fairly evenly between Venezuela, the United States and Europe.
